items.stem: “Am I going back to a smartphone? Honestly, yes; I need it for work.” These lines are from a blog. Explain who the text is written for and why, referring to one feature of its style.
items.answer: Audience: readers of a lifestyle blog, mostly young adults. Purpose: to recount and reflect on a personal experience. Feature: direct address to readers, which suits this audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark audience (readers of a lifestyle blog, mostly young adults); 1 mark purpose (to recount and reflect on a personal experience); 1 mark for a relevant feature with brief explanation (e.g. direct address to readers).

items.stem: Answer each question about this extract from the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’, making as many points as the marks indicate. “Yet many teenagers report three or more hours a night, squeezed in between sport, chores and part-time jobs. I am not arguing for banning homework altogether. … Our children’s evenings are not an extension of the school day.” Why does the writer include this sentence? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. [2]
items.answer: To appear reasonable and avoid seeming extreme, which makes the argument more persuasive to teachers and parents. Evidence: ‘I am not arguing for banning homework altogether.’ – it is a concession before the main proposal.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: to appear reasonable and avoid seeming extreme, which makes the argument more persuasive to teachers and parents. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘I am not arguing for banning homework altogether.’ (it is a concession before the main proposal) [2]

items.stem: Task: “Imagine you are one of the two teenagers who were rescued. You write a letter of thanks to Sipho.” A student’s response includes this sentence copied from the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: ‘Someone came for my father once, years ago. I suppose I am paying it back.’ Explain why this only repeats the passage, and suggest how the student could develop the idea.
items.answer: It retells the text without interpreting it, so it shows little R3 development. Development: a wish to pay the kindness forward too.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: recognises repetition/lifting; 1 mark: plausible development (a wish to pay the kindness forward too); further mark for linking it to the role and purpose.

items.stem: You are writing a summary of the progress made since the flood and the problems that remain, based on the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’. Which of these sentences contains a relevant point?
options: Three months after the River Kali burst its banks, recovery in the River District is uneven.
The regional government says it will publish its decision by the end of the year.
A survey by the traders’ association found that one in five shops has not reopened, and many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage.
Engineers have recommended raising the flood wall by one metre and restoring wetlands upstream to slow the water in future.
items.answer: A survey by the traders’ association found that one in five shops has not reopened, and many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage.
items.markingKey: It gives the point that a fifth of shops still shut; the other sentences do not address the focus.

items.stem: What does reading objective R1 require you to do?
options: Demonstrate understanding of explicit meanings
Select and use information for specific purposes
Analyse, evaluate and develop facts, ideas and opinions, using appropriate support from the text
Demonstrate understanding of how writers achieve effects and influence readers
items.answer: Demonstrate understanding of explicit meanings
items.markingKey: R1: demonstrate understanding of explicit meanings.

items.stem: In the review ‘Review: The Floating Museum’ the writer writes: ‘Less successful is the upper deck, which is crammed with glass cases of maps and instruments labelled in tiny print.’ A student commented on ‘crammed’: ‘The word crammed is a verb and it makes you want to read on.’ (a) Explain why the student’s comment would gain few marks. (b) Write a better analysis of ‘crammed’. (c) Explain the connotations of ‘star attraction’ in ‘The lower deck is the star attraction: a dimly lit gallery where a full-size whale skeleton hangs above visitors’ heads, slowly revolving as if still swimming.’, and how it adds to the same impression.
items.answer: (a) It is general: it does not explain the meaning of the word in context or its connotations, and the comment could apply to any word. (b) ‘Crammed’ suggests too many cases squeezed into too little space, conveying a cluttered, uninviting room. (c) ‘Star attraction’ borrows the language of shows to present the lower deck as the highlight everyone comes to see.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: no meaning/connotation; 1 mark: generic comment [2] (b) meaning in context; connotation (cluttered overcrowding); effect [3] (c) connotation (the most impressive highlight); link to overall impression [2]

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: “Research suggests that for primary pupils homework makes little difference to achievement, while for older students modest amounts — around an hour a night — can help. … What I object to is busywork: tasks set because a timetable says so, not because anyone will learn from them.” (a) Give the meaning of ‘busywork’ as it is used in the text. (b) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘busywork’. (c) Give the meaning of ‘modest’ as it is used in the text. (d) Identify the clue in the surrounding words that helps you understand ‘modest’. (e) Suggest a word that could replace ‘busywork’ without changing the meaning, and explain why it fits.
items.answer: (a) Tasks that keep people occupied without any real purpose. (b) It is defined as tasks set ‘not because anyone will learn from them’. (c) Moderate; not large. (d) It is explained as ‘around an hour a night’. (e) A synonym meaning tasks that keep people occupied without any real purpose.
items.markingKey: (a) Tasks that keep people occupied without any real purpose (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) it is defined as tasks set ‘not because anyone will learn from them’ [1] (c) Moderate; not large (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (d) it is explained as ‘around an hour a night’ [1] (e) synonym that fits the sentence; brief justification [2]

items.stem: Read the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: “Sipho Ndlovu has been called out 212 times in eleven years with the Drakensberg mountain rescue team, and he still keeps his boots by the front door. ‘The phone can ring at three in the morning,’ he says. ‘You have perhaps ten minutes to be in the truck.’ Like the rest of the team, he is an unpaid volunteer; by day he teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. Most call-outs, he explains, are not dramatic falls but simple mistakes: hikers who set off too late, who underestimate how quickly the weather changes, or who rely on a phone battery that dies on the mountain. The worst night he remembers was a search for two teenagers in thick cloud. ‘We found them at dawn, cold and frightened but alive. I have never been so tired or so happy.’ Asked why he continues, he shrugs. ‘Someone came for my father once, years ago. I suppose I am paying it back.’” Answer the questions. (a) How many times has Sipho been called out, and over how long? (b) What is Sipho’s paid job? (c) When were the two teenagers found? (d) What does this detail suggest about Sipho’s commitment? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. (e) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘paying it back’.
items.answer: (a) 212 times in eleven years. (b) He teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. (c) At dawn. (d) He is always ready to go and is still fully committed after many years. Evidence: ‘he still keeps his boots by the front door’ – ‘still’ after eleven years and 212 call-outs. (e) Repaying a kindness by helping others in turn.
items.markingKey: (a) 212 times in eleven years. [1] (b) He teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. [1] (c) At dawn. [1] (d) 1 mark: he is always ready to go and is still fully committed after many years. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘he still keeps his boots by the front door’ (‘still’ after eleven years and 212 call-outs) [2] (e) Repaying a kindness by helping others in turn; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2]

items.stem: Rewrite each sentence in a register suited to the audience named, keeping its meaning. (a) Rewrite ‘Your floodlights are seriously messing up our sky, sort it out!’ for the town council. (b) Rewrite ‘I am writing to inform you that the journey was extremely unpleasant.’ for a close friend, in a letter. (c) Explain how the intended audience shaped the choices you made when rewriting.
items.answer: (a) I would ask the council to reconsider how long the floodlights remain on each night. (b) You won’t believe the journey I’ve just had — it was awful! (c) For the town council: polite modal ‘would ask’, precise vocabulary, no slang. For a close friend, in a letter: contractions, exclamation and a chatty tone suit a friend.
items.markingKey: (a) appropriate formal register, meaning kept [2] (b) appropriate informal register, meaning kept [2] (c) specific choice of vocabulary or tone linked to the audience [2]

items.stem: A student writing a summary of the common mistakes that lead to rescues and what volunteering involves (the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’) wrote: ‘They must be ready within minutes – this is basically what the writer is really trying to say in this part of the passage.’ Explain why this sentence would lose marks, and rewrite it.
items.answer: It loses marks because it uses many unnecessary words before the point, wasting the word limit. Rewrite: They must be ready within minutes.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: identifies the fault (pad: it uses many unnecessary words before the point, wasting the word limit); 1 mark: concise own-words rewrite – they must be ready within minutes.

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’: “As a child I told everyone I preferred sandcastles; as a teenager I said swimming was boring; as an adult I simply stopped going to the beach. So when I signed up for beginners’ lessons at the age of forty, I expected to be laughed at.” What do the writer’s excuses suggest about how they felt when younger? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: They were ashamed of not being able to swim and hid it behind excuses. Evidence: ‘as a teenager I said swimming was boring’ – a different excuse at each age suggests a cover story rather than a real preference.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: they were ashamed of not being able to swim and hid it behind excuses. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘as a teenager I said swimming was boring’ (a different excuse at each age suggests a cover story rather than a real preference) [2]

items.stem: Read these lines from a short story: “Only the old mango by the well remained. ‘Planted it the year your mother was born,’ he told me, though I had heard the story a hundred times.” Identify the likely audience and purpose, and explain how one feature of the writing shows this.
items.answer: Audience: general readers of fiction. Purpose: to entertain readers with a story. Feature: third- or first-person narration of events, which suits this audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark audience (general readers of fiction); 1 mark purpose (to entertain readers with a story); 1 mark for a relevant feature with brief explanation (e.g. third- or first-person narration of events).

items.stem: Which word has the most positive connotations for a home?
options: building
property
unit
haven
items.answer: haven
items.markingKey: ‘haven’ suggests safety and comfort.

items.stem: Which response best develops the detail ‘the bus left two hours late’ in role?
options: The bus was late. It was late.
For us locals a late bus is normal, but I could see the visitor’s patience draining with every glass of tea.
The bus left two hours late.
There was a bus.
items.answer: For us locals a late bus is normal, but I could see the visitor’s patience draining with every glass of tea.
items.markingKey: It infers a viewpoint and feelings from the detail.

items.stem: A student’s Paper 1 marks are broken down by objective: Q1 retrieval 8/10 (R1), Q1 inference 6/10 (R2), Q2 summary content 9/10 (R5), Q3 language task 8/20 (R4), Q4 reading 5/10 (R3). (a) Convert each score to a percentage. (b) Identify the two weakest objectives. (c) For each of the two weakest objectives, set a specific target and describe one practice activity. (d) Evaluate whether the student should spend more revision time on Question 3 or Question 1, using the figures.
items.answer: (a) R1 (Q1 retrieval) 80%, R2 (Q1 inference) 60%, R5 (Q2 summary content) 90%, R4 (Q3 language) 40%, R3 (Q4 reading) 50% (b) R4 (Q3 language) and R3 (Q4 reading) (c) R4: demonstrate understanding of how writers achieve effects and influence readers – targeted practice with model answers; R3: analyse, evaluate and develop facts, ideas and opinions, using appropriate support from the text – timed practice and self-marking against the mark scheme. (d) Compare the R4 percentage with the average of R1 and R2: the lower area, with more marks available, should get more time.
items.markingKey: (a) all five correct [2] (b) R4 (Q3 language); R3 (Q4 reading) [1] (c) 1 mark per relevant target + 1 per suitable activity [4] (d) uses figures; reasoned judgement [2]

items.stem: These notes for a summary of how visitors can protect the reef and its wildlife (the leaflet ‘Visiting the Coral Reef Responsibly’) are in a random order: (1) Do not chase or feed animals. (2) Do not touch or stand on coral. (3) Use licensed guides whose boats do not anchor on the reef. (4) Stay three metres from turtles and rays. (5) Take litter, especially plastic, home. (6) Use reef-safe sun cream. Arrange them into a logical order, group them, and write the summary as a short paragraph using suitable connectives.
items.answer: Order: protecting the coral first, then protecting the animals. Model paragraph: To protect the coral, visitors should never touch or stand on it, should use only reef-safe sun cream and should book trips with licensed guides, whose boats moor rather than anchor on the reef. To protect the animals, they should keep at least three metres from turtles and rays, never chase or feed them, and take all litter, especially plastic bags, home.
items.markingKey: Mark points: logical grouping (protecting the coral / protecting the animals); appropriate connectives (e.g. ‘In addition’, ‘However’); all points included in own words; continuous prose.

items.stem: In the report ‘Canteen Food Waste Report’, the writer uses the phrase ‘safe to use’. Two students explained it. Student A wrote: ‘It means that safe to use.’ Student B wrote: ‘Still fit to eat.’ (a) Explain which answer would gain credit, and why. (b) Using your own words, explain what the writer means by ‘at peak times’. (c) Give one piece of advice to Student A for answering ‘own words’ questions. (d) Give the meaning of ‘accounted for’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) Student B: A simply repeats the writer’s words, so shows no understanding; B explains the meaning in their own words. (b) When the canteen is at its busiest. (c) Work out the meaning, then express it with different words (synonyms), keeping the same sense; check no key word from the phrase is repeated. (d) Made up (a proportion of).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: B; 1 mark: A repeats/lifts the key words [2] (b) when the canteen is at its busiest [2] (c) any sensible, specific advice [1] (d) Made up (a proportion of) (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: Annotate this extract from the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’ for a task on the difficulties of the journey and the moments that made it bearable. List each relevant point in a short note of your own. Then group your points under two headings. “The bus was supposed to leave at seven. It left at nine, after the driver had finished his tea, his second tea and a long conversation with a man selling oranges. Every seat was taken, and the aisle was soon packed with sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a schoolboy who fell asleep standing up. The road climbed in hairpin bends, and on the outside of each bend there was nothing at all — no barrier, no verge, only a sheer drop to a river that glittered like a thread of tin far below. I gripped the seat in front so hard my knuckles turned white. The woman beside me noticed.”
items.answer: The bus left two hours late; It was extremely overcrowded; The road ran along terrifying unprotected drops. Headings: difficulties / comforts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per relevant point (max 3): the bus left two hours late; it was extremely overcrowded; the road ran along terrifying unprotected drops. 1 mark for sensible grouping. No credit for copied irrelevant detail.

items.stem: Explain why this sentence from the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’ should be annotated for a task on the common mistakes that lead to rescues and what volunteering involves, and write a brief margin note for it: ‘Most call-outs, he explains, are not dramatic falls but simple mistakes: hikers who set off too late, who underestimate how quickly the weather changes, or who rely on a phone battery that dies on the mountain.’
items.answer: It is relevant because it shows that they rely on phones whose batteries fail. Margin note: “they rely on phones whose batteries fail”.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: links the sentence to the focus (the common mistakes that lead to rescues and what volunteering involves); 1 mark: concise own-words note, e.g. “they rely on phones whose batteries fail”.

items.stem: Read this extract from the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’: “I understand why many readers welcomed them; nobody wants to walk through a dark park feeling unsafe. … Light pollution is not merely a hobby problem for people like me.” Why does the writer say light pollution is ‘not merely a hobby problem’? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: She expects readers to dismiss her as a stargazer, so she widens the issue to show it affects everyone. Evidence: ‘not merely a hobby problem’ – she then lists effects on residents, birds and money.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: she expects readers to dismiss her as a stargazer, so she widens the issue to show it affects everyone. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘not merely a hobby problem’ (she then lists effects on residents, birds and money) [2]

items.stem: Explain why a summary should not include the writer’s examples or quotations.
items.answer: Examples and quotations illustrate a point but are not points themselves; including them wastes words and suggests lifting rather than selecting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: they illustrate rather than add new points; 1 mark: waste words within the limit / show lifting. [2]

items.stem: If all four Paper 1 questions carry equal marks, how many marks is each worth?
What is bias?
options: A balanced weighing of both sides
A list of facts with no opinions
A one-sided presentation that favours one viewpoint
A type of summary
items.answer: A one-sided presentation that favours one viewpoint
items.markingKey: Bias = unbalanced selection or language.

items.stem: Read this extract from the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “He moved slowly between the rows, touching each trunk as if he were taking attendance at a school register. … Its bark was cracked like a dry riverbed, and its lowest branch dipped so close to the ground that I could sit on it without jumping.” Explain how the writer uses imagery and sound to create Grandfather’s grief and love for the orchard. Refer closely to specific words and phrases and explain their effects.
items.answer: Model points: ‘Its bark was cracked like a dry riverbed’ (simile: the simile compares the bark to a parched river, suggesting great age, endurance and thirst; the tree, like Grandfather, is old and has survived hardship.) ‘as if he were taking attendance at a school register’ (simile: comparing Grandfather to a teacher calling the register suggests care, responsibility and routine; it also makes the missing trees feel like absent pupils.)
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (language task: how the writer conveys Grandfather’s grief and love for the orchard). Top band (8–10): a wide range of well-chosen words and phrases, including imagery, with precise explanation of meaning in context and of connotations and effects; analysis is developed, not just identified. Middle band (5–7): relevant choices with some explanation of meaning and effect, but some comments are general or partly descriptive. Lower band (1–4): some relevant selection, with explanations that are general (e.g. ‘makes it interesting’) or that repeat the words. Indicative content: ‘Its bark was cracked like a dry riverbed’ – simile: the simile compares the bark to a parched river, suggesting great age, endurance and thirst; the tree, like Grandfather, is old and has survived hardship. ‘as if he were taking attendance at a school register’ – simile: comparing Grandfather to a teacher calling the register suggests care, responsibility and routine; it also makes the missing trees feel like absent pupils.

items.stem: Read this extract from the blog ‘Street Food Fridays’: “I have burned my fingers on them every single week and I regret nothing. Not everything is perfect. There are not enough bins, and by nine the ground is littered with paper plates.” (a) Identify the text type. (b) Identify the intended audience. (c) State the main purpose of the text. (d) Give two features typical of this text type, supporting one with a quotation from the extract. (e) Explain how the register (level of formality) suits the audience.
items.answer: (a) Blog. (b) Readers of a food and travel blog. (c) To recount and reflect on a personal experience. (d) Direct address to readers; humour and personal anecdote. (e) The register suits readers of a food and travel blog: personal and engaging.
items.markingKey: (a) blog [1] (b) readers of a food and travel blog (accept reasonable equivalents) [1] (c) to recount and reflect on a personal experience [1] (d) 1 mark per relevant feature; quotation must support the feature [2] (e) identifies register; links to audience [2]

items.stem: Read the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: “Every evening, in millions of homes, the same battle is fought over the kitchen table. Parents nag, children sulk, and a worksheet on fractions somehow takes two hours. It is time we asked whether homework is worth the misery. The evidence is far less clear than many teachers assume. Research suggests that for primary pupils homework makes little difference to achievement, while for older students modest amounts — around an hour a night — can help. Beyond that, the benefits fall away and stress rises. Yet many teenagers report three or more hours a night, squeezed in between sport, chores and part-time jobs. I am not arguing for banning homework altogether. Reading for pleasure, practising a musical instrument or revising for a test are valuable habits. What I object to is busywork: tasks set because a timetable says so, not because anyone will learn from them. Schools should set less homework, set it better and, above all, explain why it matters. Our children’s evenings are not an extension of the school day.” Answer the questions. (a) According to the research, how much homework can help older students? (b) How much homework do many teenagers report doing? (c) How long does the worksheet on fractions take? (d) What impression does this create of homework time at home? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. (e) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘the benefits fall away’.
items.answer: (a) Around an hour a night. (b) Three or more hours a night. (c) Two hours. (d) It is tense and unhappy, a regular source of conflict within families. Evidence: ‘Parents nag, children sulk’ – ‘nag’ and ‘sulk’ suggest irritation on both sides. (e) The advantages disappear.
items.markingKey: (a) Around an hour a night. [1] (b) Three or more hours a night. [1] (c) Two hours. [1] (d) 1 mark: it is tense and unhappy, a regular source of conflict within families. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘Parents nag, children sulk’ (‘nag’ and ‘sulk’ suggest irritation on both sides) [2] (e) The advantages disappear; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2]

items.stem: These notes for a summary of the problems caused by the floodlights and the solution suggested (the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’) are in a random order: (1) They waste public money. (2) They confuse migrating birds. (3) They hide the stars. (4) They keep residents awake. (5) Use motion-sensor lights that come on only when needed. (6) Lights stay on four hours after the park closes. Arrange them into a logical order, group them, and write the summary as a short paragraph using suitable connectives.
items.answer: Order: problems first, then solution. Model paragraph: The floodlights stay on until 2 a.m., four hours after the park closes. As a result, the stars are hidden, nearby residents’ sleep is disturbed, migrating birds are confused and public money is wasted. The writer proposes motion-sensor lighting, which would come on only when someone is actually in the park.
items.markingKey: Mark points: logical grouping (problems / solution); appropriate connectives (e.g. ‘In addition’, ‘However’); all points included in own words; continuous prose.
